title: Debt-to-Income Ratio: The Number That Decides Your Budget
description: Lenders care about your debt-to-income ratio as much as your credit score. Learn how DTI is calculated, what counts, and how to improve it before applying.
keywords: how much house can I afford
image_alt: A small white and red model house on a wooden table

faq.a: It's your total monthly debt payments, including the new housing payment, divided by your gross monthly income. Lenders use it to judge whether a payment is sustainable.

faq.q: Do utilities and groceries count toward DTI?
faq.a: No. DTI counts debts that appear on your credit report or are legally owed, such as car loans, student loans, card minimums, child support, and the new housing payment.

faq.q: How can I lower my DTI quickly?
faq.a: Paying off a small installment loan, paying down revolving balances, or adding a qualifying co-borrower can lower DTI. Talk with a loan officer before moving money so you don't create a documentation problem.

body_html:
Ask most people what matters for a mortgage and they'll say credit score. It matters. But the number that usually decides how much you can borrow is quieter: your debt-to-income ratio, or DTI.

I've seen buyers with excellent credit come in under their target price because of a car payment, and buyers with average credit qualify comfortably because they carry almost no debt. Here's how DTI works and how to put it on your side.

How DTI is calculated

The math is simple. Add up your monthly debt payments, including the new housing payment, and divide by your gross monthly income, meaning income before taxes.

The housing payment includes principal, interest, property taxes, homeowners insurance, HOA dues, and any mortgage insurance. That's why the same loan amount can produce very different DTIs in two neighborhoods with different tax rates or HOA fees.

Lenders often look at two versions:

  • Front-end ratio: housing payment only, divided by income.
  • Back-end ratio: housing payment plus all other monthly debts, divided by income. This is the one that usually drives approval.

What counts as debt, and what doesn't

Counts toward DTIUsually doesn't count
Car loans and leasesUtilities and phone bills
Student loan paymentsGroceries and gas
Credit card minimum paymentsCar and health insurance
Personal loans and installment plansSubscriptions and memberships
Child support and alimony you payRetirement contributions

Two details trip people up. First, student loans in deferment still usually count, using a calculated payment based on program rules. Second, a "buy now, pay later" plan or a co-signed loan for a family member can count even if someone else makes the payments.

What income counts

Lenders want income that's stable and likely to continue. W-2 salary is straightforward. Overtime, bonus, and commission usually need a two-year history. Self-employed income is typically averaged from tax returns after business deductions, which is why some business owners qualify for less than they expect. If that's you, alternative documentation like a bank statement loan may be worth a look.

Practical ways to improve your DTI

  1. Pay off small installment debts. A loan with a few payments left can sometimes be paid off to remove it from the calculation.
  2. Pay down credit cards. Lower balances mean lower minimum payments, and often a better credit score too.
  3. Hold off on new financing. A new car or furniture on credit before closing can undo an approval.
  4. Add a co-borrower. A spouse or family member with qualifying income can change the picture, as long as you both understand the obligation.
  5. Adjust the target. A lower price point, a property with lower HOA dues, or a larger down payment all reduce the housing side of the ratio.

Before you move money around, call your loan officer. Large deposits and transfers need paper trails, and the order you do things in can matter.

Qualifying versus comfortable

The maximum DTI a program allows isn't a recommendation. Lenders don't know about daycare, travel, or the fact that you want to keep funding your retirement. I always encourage clients to build a real monthly budget around the full housing payment and decide where they feel comfortable, then shop in that range.

The best approval is the one that still lets you sleep at night six months after you move in.

A simple example

Numbers make this clearer, so here's a simplified illustration using round figures, not an offer or a quote. Imagine a household with gross monthly income of $15,000. They have a car payment of $600 and student loan payments of $400, so $1,000 in existing debt.

  • If the full housing payment on the home they want is $5,000, total debts are $6,000. That's a back-end DTI of 40%.
  • If they pay off the car loan before applying, total debts drop to $5,400, or 36%.
  • If they instead choose a home with a $4,500 housing payment and keep the car, total debts are $5,500, or about 37%.

Small changes on either side of the ratio move the result. That's why it's worth modeling a few versions with your loan officer before you start touring homes.

How DTI limits differ by loan type

Each loan program sets its own approach. Some use automated underwriting systems that weigh DTI alongside credit, reserves, and down payment, so a borrower with strong compensating factors may be approved at a higher ratio than someone with a thinner profile. Others apply firmer caps. Non-QM programs may calculate income differently altogether.

The practical point: there isn't one universal DTI limit. If one program's ratio is too tight for your situation, another may fit. Comparing options across lenders is one of the advantages of working with a mortgage broker.

The takeaway

Your DTI turns your income and debts into a single number lenders can compare. Know what counts, clean up what you can before applying, and pick a payment that fits your life, not just the guideline.
